explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The writer says we have “…a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God…” The other high priests in this passage are appointed from among men. This one went through the heavens. I'd love to see another résumé with that line on it.

I get the guess, friend, since this passage is full of priest talk. But the writer says Jesus “…has passed through the heavens…” That's a much bigger trip than a walk through any courtyard. Next time, aim a little higher. Way higher.

The Jordan is a real river with real Bible history, but it isn't in this verse. The writer says our great high priest “…has passed through the heavens…” That's a bigger trip than wading across anything. I'd have gotten my apron soaked at the Jordan, and this trip is nowhere near that.

explanations.answer: Hold firmly to what we profess
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The writer says, “…let us hold firmly to what we profess.” He says it because we already have this great high priest. Think of grabbing a hot tray with a thin oven mitt. You don't loosen up, you hold on.

No waiting, friend. The writer says “…since we have a great high priest…” We already have one. Waiting for another would be like standing by the oven for a batch that's already out and cooling on the rack.

explanations.answer: Offer our gifts at the temple
explanations.explanation: Gifts and sacrifices do come up in this passage, but that's the job of the high priest in Hebrews 5:1. The instruction in this verse is “…let us hold firmly to what we profess.” So the writer is telling us to hold on to our profession. That's a different job from carrying gifts.

Close, baker, but the text says the opposite. The writer says, “For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses…” Read it slowly and the double negative lands on good news. Our high priest is able to sympathize.

Yes, baker, it's False. The writer says, “For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses…” So our high priest is able to sympathize, and He doesn't just nod politely. The writer goes on to say He “…was tempted in every way that we are…”

That's right. The verse says He “…was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin.” Every way, and still without sin. My apron has never come out of a batch that clean, and I'm not even tempted by anything but the dough.
The text doesn't say that, friend. It says Jesus “…was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin.” Not once, not a little bit. That's the whole point of the word “yet.”

That's what the writer says about other high priests, who offer sacrifices for their own sins (Hebrews 5:3). Here the writer says of Jesus that He was “…without sin.” So this answer fits the other priests, not Him. Good thing you've got another look at the verse coming.
You got it, baker. The writer says, “Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence…” No tiptoeing, no sneaking in the back. It's a throne of grace, so you can walk up like you belong.

A throne can make a person want to stare at the floor, I get it. But the writer says to approach “…with confidence…” and that's a head-up kind of word. Notice what kind of throne it is, too. It's a throne of grace.

I think a throne sounds like a knee-knocking kind of place. But the writer says, “Let us then approach the throne of grace with confidence…” The word is confidence, not trembling. And again, it's a throne of grace.

Right, baker. The verse says we approach “…so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in our time of need.” Mercy and grace, both on offer. And the help comes in our time of need, which is when we want it most.

I see why a throne makes you think of that, friend. But the verse says we approach the throne of grace so that we “…may receive mercy…” What waits there is mercy and grace to help. Judgment isn't in the sentence.

Riches would be nice, I won't lie. But the verse says we receive mercy and “…find grace to help us in our time of need.” It's help for a time of need, not a lottery window. Mercy is the word the writer picked.

That's right, baker. The writer says, “Every high priest is appointed from among men to represent them in matters relating to God…” So he comes from the people he stands in front of. He's one of them, picked to represent them.

It's True, friend. The writer says, “Every high priest is appointed from among men to represent them in matters relating to God…” He comes from among the people, not from somewhere else. His job is to represent them in matters relating to God.
You got it, baker. The verse says a high priest is appointed “…to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.” Gifts and sacrifices, that's the job. And it's for sins, which is the heavy part of the verse.
A high priest as a worship leader, I like the picture. But the verse says he is appointed “…to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.” This job isn't a talent show. The word is sacrifices.

Coins are a fair guess, since gifts can feel like money. But the verse says “…gifts and sacrifices for sins.” Gifts is already in the sentence, and it doesn't say what they are. The word that fills the blank is sacrifices.

explanations.answer: He is subject to weakness himself
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The writer says, “He is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and misguided, since he himself is subject to weakness.” The reason is right there in the verse. He knows weakness from the inside, so he can be gentle.

explanations.answer: He was trained to be patient
explanations.explanation: Patience training sounds like a good program, friend. But the verse gives a different reason, “…since he himself is subject to weakness.” The writer doesn't mention any training. It's his own weakness that helps him deal gently.

explanations.answer: The law orders him to be kind
explanations.explanation: The writer doesn't mention a law ordering kindness here, baker. He says the high priest is able to deal gently “…since he himself is subject to weakness.” That's the reason in the text. I think it's a nicer reason than an order, too.

Not quite, baker. The writer says, “That is why he is obligated to offer sacrifices for his own sins, as well as for the sins of the people.” So the sacrifices cover his sins too, not only the people's. He's subject to weakness himself, remember.

Yes, it's False. The writer says the high priest “…is obligated to offer sacrifices for his own sins, as well as for the sins of the people.” That's two lists, and his own name is on one of them. It fits with what the writer just said about him being subject to weakness.

explanations.answer: He must be called by God
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The writer says, “No one takes this honor upon himself; he must be called by God…” So the honor is given, not grabbed. Nobody gets this one by being the first in line.
The writer says the opposite, friend. “No one takes this honor upon himself…” Nobody gets to walk in, slap on a name tag and announce it. The next part says he “…must be called by God…”
A vote sounds fair, I get it. But the writer says, “No one takes this honor upon himself; he must be called by God…” The text doesn't mention the people choosing. The call comes from God.
You got it, baker. The writer says a high priest “…must be called by God, just as Aaron was.” Aaron is the high priest the writer points to as an example. Called, not self-appointed.

Elijah, the prophet (1 Kings 18:36), is a great name, friend. But he isn't the one this verse picks. The writer says a high priest “…must be called by God, just as Aaron was.” Aaron is the name in the verse.
Samuel, a prophet of the LORD (1 Samuel 3:20), is another great name. But this verse doesn't use it. The writer says “…called by God, just as Aaron was.” So the answer is Aaron.
The text says the opposite, baker. “So also Christ did not take upon Himself the glory of becoming a high priest…” He didn't grab it. The verse says He was called, just like Aaron.

Yes, it's False. The writer says, “So also Christ did not take upon Himself the glory of becoming a high priest, but He was called…” He didn't take it. He was called. It's the same way the writer said a high priest receives the honor.

The verse says something much bigger, baker. God says, “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of God Most High (Genesis 14:18). The word is forever, not just a lifetime on earth.
That's right, it's False. The verse says, “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” Forever beats any contract I've ever heard of. It doesn't stop when His time on earth does.
That's right, baker. The writer says Jesus prayed “…to the One who could save Him from death…” I think this one hurts a little. The writer says it plainly, and it comes with loud cries and tears.

Shame isn't in this verse, friend. The writer says Jesus offered prayers and petitions “…to the One who could save Him from death…” The word is death. It's a heavy one, and the verse doesn't soften it.

Exile is a big word in other parts of the Bible, but not here, baker. This verse says Jesus prayed “…to the One who could save Him from death…” The text names death. That's the word that fills the blank.
You got it, baker. The writer says, “…and He was heard because of His reverence.” Loud cries and tears, and He was heard. The text says it plainly.
The verse says otherwise, friend. After the prayers and the tears, the writer says, “…and He was heard because of His reverence.” So He was heard. That's the sentence to hold on to.
That's the reason, baker. The writer says, “…and He was heard because of His reverence.” The verse gives that one reason and no other. Reverence is the word the writer picks.
There's no stopwatch in this verse, friend. The writer says nothing about how long Jesus prayed. What it says is, “…He was heard because of His reverence.”
Fasting doesn't come up in this verse, baker. The writer gives one reason, “…He was heard because of His reverence.” So the answer is reverence. I'm sticking to what the verse actually says.

That's right, baker. The writer says, “Although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered.” That's a surprising line, and I won't dress it up. The verse says suffered, and that's the word.

Preaching is a good guess, friend, since Jesus taught a lot. But this verse says, “Although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered.” The word in the blank is suffered. Preached isn't in the sentence.
Built would be an easy guess, baker, but it isn't what the verse says. The writer says Jesus “…learned obedience from what He suffered.” Suffered is the word. Keep your eyes on that one.
You got it, baker. The writer says, “…He became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey Him…” All who obey Him. That's who the verse names.

explanations.answer: All who were born in Israel
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't mention where anyone was born, friend. It says, “…the source of eternal salvation to all who obey Him…” The group the writer names is all who obey Him.

Sacrifices belong to the earthly high priests, baker. The writer described those jobs back in Hebrews 5:1. But this verse says Jesus became the source of eternal salvation “…to all who obey Him…” Obeying Him is the answer.
